items.note: Story 1: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president to 1911, creamery built 1891.
Story 1 quotes Article VII: paid on pounds of butterfat not weight of milk; 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.
Calls Article VII 'the hinge of everything that follows' but never states that payment by fat is what made a wrong test cost money; no by-weight counterfactual anywhere in Section A.

Effie Loomis secretary/minutes (Stories 1, 5), Teague bookkeeper from 1905 (Story 6), Hobart Sill buttermaker at Larrow Green (Stories 2, 3). Effie's 1901 start missing but the item's core officers are named with roles.
Section A never states Selby Vose is Gideon's son nor that he became manager in 1913. Both appear only in B3 and E, which cannot travel into Section A.

Story 6 names the 'station gain' line, its shape (fat arriving heavier than credited, ~5.25 percent, 'as usual' in the wording). Origin misdated to 1905 (r05's planted error) - charged as a corruption deduction, not here.
Story 2: Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up the valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed from Larrow Green (via Sill).

Story 2 gives the bench routine (weigh, composite sample over ten days, charge the pipette to its mark, acid, spin, read the column); Story 7 adds the neck ruled for the full charge; Story 6 has cream going to Larrow Green. Skim return not stated.
Ammon & Sons of Tarnet sold the 1897 outfit (Story 8); in use from 1 May 1897 (Story 2). Invoice date 14 April 1897 absent from Section A but the item's core fact is present.
Story 8: $77.93 for six dozen pipettes, twelve dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight; 17.6 cc mark in Story 7.
Story 7 states the flat, unchanging 26-year gap independent of season or operator; 0.19 named in Story 3.
Section A never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette or that none existed in the county. The burette point appears only in Story 7 as the 1958 method and in F1 (Section F).
Story 2: tester at Ostrey Hollow 29 seasons, 1896-1924, dismissed 30 April 1925. Birth year absent (context).
Story 2: five columns, one hand, corrections crossed and initialed, never overwritten.

The summary leaf's two figures (1896 at 3.80, 3.61 from 1898 within three hundredths since) never appear in Section A. 3.61 appears in Story 8 only as the Ostrey Hollow record; the 1896 average is nowhere.
The 1911 interval is only cross-referenced in Section A ('see Story 6/D1'); its dates, the 3.80 run and the question mark are stated only in D1 and F1, which cannot travel into Section A.
Story 4: Orra Brant married Keddie; her brother Emmet was the largest place on Hessel Bottom and the station's largest patron; Keddie tested his own brother-in-law's milk.

1919 circular over the manager's signature (Stories 3, 4) and Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement that he tested faithfully for 29 seasons and never took a pound of cream (Story 5). 'Cannot say why the figures are what they are' not reproduced.
Story 2: died 1934, still under suspicion. Impoundment and the 1959 transfer absent (context).
Story 4/8: six farms on Hessel Bottom, Emmet Brant's the largest; wet/bog meadow established in Story 3.
Brant's private weigh book appears nowhere in the entire answer sheet - not the 1 January 1897 start, not the two scales agreeing, not the disposal of short weight.

1902 complaints correctly stated, but Story 3 then prints the Hollow-vs-Green complaint gap as '0.17 / 0.19 / 0.21' and picks 0.19 as best corroborated - exactly the conflation of the visible 0.17 gap with the true 0.19 shortfall that the key charges this item for.
Story 3: 1908 committee under Nyle Grigg, sampling confined to January-March, hay blamed - stated as a theory 'advanced, none correct', not as fact.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at 3.42) and the proportional loss falling harder on the richer herds appear only in C2 and F1, never in Section A.
The weigh book's descent (Roy Brant 1929, lent to Ivy 1958, Hazel after 1962) is absent from the whole sheet.
Story 8: Alder Corners Cheese Company, over Redlow Ridge, in Vessey County, Jerome Cudd. Founding year not gating.
Story 8: from 1915, four of the six Hessel Bottom farms hauled summer-flush milk there, returning to Ostrey Hollow the rest of the year.
REQUIRED line met with three of four: another county (Vessey), his own independent glassware, his own book.
Story 8: the same four men's milk ran 3.78-3.82 at Alder Corners against Ostrey Hollow's 3.61, sixteen seasons 1915-1930.
Story 8 draws the inference: the same milk on entirely independent equipment 'proving the milk itself was never poor', years before the crate was found.
Story 8: Rosalie is Jerome's daughter and supplied the figures to Ivy Keddie by letter in 1958. 1941-1962 tenure absent (context).
Strawn is named as state inspector with his circuit notebooks, but the span is given as 'from 1908 on' (Story 3, repeated in F2) - the planted NT-23 value. 1907-1936 never stated.
Story 3: Strawn's notebooks record testing for added water at every visit and never finding any.
Section A has only 'condemned by the state inspector in 1923'. The 12 June date and the burette check appear only in C5 and E.
That Strawn wrote no figure for the deficiency and made no report beyond the condemnation is nowhere in the sheet.

Section A carries the 1924 average only as Vose's claim of 3.90; the replacement order of 28 June, the July installation and the 1924 average of 3.80 never appear in Section A (3.80 for 1924 is resolved only in Section E).

The only loft statement in Section A is the 1958 finding, which is scored at A8.3; the crate's 1923 journey to the loft and the notebooks' path to the state office and the 1947 college library are not stated. Per the key's no-double-scoring rule the shared element takes one item, not both.
Story 5: 'The patrons petitioned in January 1925.'
Story 5: three-man board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March-4 May 1925, two of the three sessions in the station's own weigh room.
Story 5: water (Vose), theft (Teague), wet hay (the reprinted 1908 report); 'the board found none of them established.'
The four-book exhibit list, and in particular Strawn's 1923 notebook being in the room and read for its other lines, is absent.
Story 5: dismissed 30 April 1925 with no finding behind it; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800, 'without admission,' charged to the station account.
Section A never states the award was one fifth of the $19,000 lost, nor that it was charged to the same account into which the loss had accumulated as 'gain'. The fifth appears only in C1(d).
Story 7: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland, working with Leland Vaught; b. 1931 in Story 4.
No statement that she assembled records that had never been in the same room, and no enumeration of the five series in Section A.
Story 7: February 1958, the loft over the old station's intake room, nine survived intact.
Story 7: 9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 cc against a 17.6 cc mark, short 0.88 cc, 95 percent of the mark.

Across Section A: 95 percent of the truth and a proportionally low reading in every test (Story 7), the recorded 3.61 against ~3.80 for the same milk (Story 8), 0.19 (Story 3), onset 1 May 1897 (Story 2) and 1923 condemnation (Story 7).

REQUIRED all four inside Section A: only the fat (76,000 lb) is there. The 40,000,000 lb of milk and the $19,000 appear only in Section C, and the identity of 76,000 lb with the sum of the ledger's station-gain entries is never asserted anywhere.
Story 7: Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, quoted, clearing him 24 years after his death and 33 after his dismissal.
Granddaughter.
Derivation given (Duncan is Ansel's son and Ivy's father) plus Falke's own appended self-correction; 'great-niece' named and rejected.
Second cousins with the full chain: Orra and Emmet siblings, Duncan and Roy first cousins, Ivy and Hazel children of first cousins.

A08 abstention correct: states the sources never resolve full vs half sibling and that it does not change the cousin arithmetic. Story 4's 'I favor Roy's account ... but the sources do not fully settle it' carries its declining qualifier in the same sentence, so no assertion.
Gideon Vose, his father; 'nephew' named and rejected.
Significance stated on the key's first alternative: the accuser was the son of the man who wrote the rule that made the station's test decisive, with a stake in defending it.

A01 abstention: 'this cannot be proven with certainty, only shown to be unsupported' and 'a family denial is not the same as documentary proof of a negative'. The lean is qualified in its own sentence, so it is a correct abstention and the item is not lost on that ground.
States what is established: two narrators assert cousinship from valley talk (Toland, Oram), Duncan denies it flatly and attributes it to a different Vose family, and the denial is not a record.
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95 exactly; 95 percent of the truth, one part in twenty. 16.27 named and rejected with a reason.
76,000 x $0.25 = $19,000; $3,800 received; 3,800/19,000 = one fifth. Both the money and the fraction.
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, with the 1910 price explicitly sourced to Roy Brant and the $90.00 alternative noted.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb actually delivered.

Names both denominators correctly: 5 percent of the fat actually delivered (76,000/1,520,000), 5.25 percent of the fat credited (76,000/1,444,000). Rounds 5.2632 to 5.25 rather than 5.26, but it is not bare and the denominators are attached the right way round, so no NT-20 error.
$77.93; $77.39 named and rejected as a transposition, noting the carrier contradicts her own quoted invoice.
Six dozen (72), each short 0.88 cc. Both required elements present; 'five dozen' rejected.

Two distinct figures with the reason: glass in service 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 ('about 26 years') against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, excluded because 1897 and 1923 are part years. Does not print the '26 years and 6 weeks' form, but gives the exact endpoints and does not collapse the two periods.
A02 abstention correct: 1896 intake cannot be determined; the catalog says it is nowhere, and Sill's 900,000 against Kyle's 1,100,000 are memories, not records.
Variable named: the measuring glass, broken 8 May 1911, borrowed measure to 10 July.
Held constant: same patrons, herds, pasture, season, acid, bottles, tester - well over three.
Rose to 3.80 for the full nine weeks and fell back to 3.61 the day the station's own measure returned. 'Six weeks' named and rejected.
Both halves: rules out herds, land, season and the tester's honesty at once; and states limits - it does not give the mechanism or size in cc, and the lender of the measure cannot be settled.
Three valid distinct reasons from the key's list (ledger surplus, 1911 interval, Strawn's clean visits), each attributed across at least three narrators.
Independence argued from separate record-keeping systems and people, and names the ledger and the 1911 interval as holding even if the crate had never been found.

A09 asserted, not abstained: 'Did the bookkeeper ever question the ledger entries...? No -' is a headline verdict, and it takes r05's 1916 conversation with Vose as established fact against the clerk's opposite account. -2 applied.
Answers the literal question yes ('Vose had actual notice well before 1923'), and elsewhere in B-G has him framing the whole history of the low tests as watering in his 1926 address.

Three of the five established facts across B-G: manager from 1913 (Section E), signed the annual station sheet every year (D3), argued watering (F1 with G's arbitration). Also notes he never questioned the station's own equipment.

A03 asserted: rests the 'yes' on Teague putting the station-gain discrepancy to Vose in 1916, and concludes 'he was informed ... and chose not to pursue the question' and 'he knew something in the numbers was persistently anomalous' - exactly the form the key's discriminator marks as asserting A03. -2 applied.

Cap reached. Qualifying rows with method stated: the 1924 average (3.90/3.85 vs 3.80), the circular's reach (eleven vs nine), Selby Vose's start as manager (1911 vs 1913), and the 1908 sampling (whole year vs Jan-Mar, resolved by the report against its own covering letter).

Cap reached and well exceeded: an explicit paragraph naming the two-narrator pairs (12 July, 16.27, five dozen, eleven pipettes, $3,500, 3.16, $77.39, 1898 glass, 'two tenths', cousin-once-removed), each with the breaker stated in the bullets above it.

A06 (whose measure was borrowed) and A10 (Article VII's adoption year) both correctly filed as unsettleable with what the sources do establish. A04 missed - the run asserts the accident pole ('almost certainly the accidental result of a reground mold') instead of abstaining.

Explicit self-refutation list: r03 Ashlin vs his own Larrow Green leaf, r11's 16.27 cascade against its own conclusion, r15's 'whole of 1908' above a three-month report, r20's 'nothing before 1900' above her 1897 invoice. Buckets sum to 9; section capped at 8 per the key.

Names the 1897 Ammon pipettes at 16.72 against 17.6, explains the neck ruled for the full charge, gives the proportional (not constant) reading and the 0.19/3.80 derivation via C1(b), and bounds both ends without anything on the farms changing.
Watering named to Selby Vose and defeated by Strawn's lactometer at every visit, never finding water.
Theft named to Teague (with Sill and Oram's father) and defeated by the ledger surplus - cream arriving heavy, the opposite of theft - plus the 1911 interval.
Bog hay named to Grigg's 1908 committee and Kepp, defeated by Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer, and by the Alder Corners book.

A07 asserted flatly: 'The 1925 board of arbitration never examined the condemned glassware ... never mentioned in any of the three sessions.' A headline verdict with no declining qualifier. -2 applied.
A05 abstention correct: gives both reported private beliefs and says 'I cannot fully reconcile these two reported private beliefs from the sources as given', repeated in Section E.
175 words against a 150-word cap.

Names no record series at all - the summary mentions a 1925 arbitration and a crate of pipettes but not the minute book, invoice, test book, weigh book, Alder Corners book, Strawn's notebooks, arbitration minutes or the ledgers.
Clean: water, theft and hay are all presented as beliefs that were 'proved none', and every headline figure used (26 years, 1897, five percent, a fifth, 1925, 1958) is correct.

Only three of the six arc elements: one part in twenty, 1897, 1958. Missing the 76,000 lb / $19,000, the 1923 condemnation date, and both names (it says 'the tester' and 'a granddaughter'). REQUIRED four.

deductions.reason: Asserts Strawn's Ordell circuit and lactometer testing as running 'from 1908' (Story 3, repeated in F2) - the planted NT-23 value; canon is 1907 on his own covering note.
Asserts the station-gain line as Teague's own device begun in 1905 (Story 6) - r05's planted X19 error; the line was carried from 1898.
Asserts that Keddie 'went up in 1895 to ready' the station (Story 2) - the planted 1895 start (X03/NT-13), unhedged, though the run correctly dates his testing from 1896.

Gullibility: A03 asserted at D3 - 'Vose had actual notice well before 1923', resting on the station-gain line put to him in 1916, and 'he knew something in the numbers was persistently anomalous and declined to investigate it'.

Gullibility: A04 asserted at F1 and Story 8 - the short lot was 'almost certainly the accidental result of a reground mold rather than any deliberate act', with the substitution pole dismissed as 'evidence-free'.
Gullibility: A07 asserted at F1 - 'The 1925 board of arbitration never examined the condemned glassware.'
Gullibility: A09 asserted at D2 - 'Did the bookkeeper ever question the ledger entries...? No', taking r05's 1916 approach to Vose as established.
